subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The 1/N Rule
description: A fast breakdown of The 1/N Rule for builders.

hook.text: Split your money equally across all options. This naive strategy beats many expert portfolios.

buildup.text: DeMiguel showed that 1/N allocation matched or beat 14 optimized portfolio models over real market data.

discovery.text: The 1/N rule: divide resources equally. It ignores all fancy analysis and works surprisingly well.

twist.text: Optimization requires accurate forecasts. Forecasts are often wrong. The simple rule avoids forecast errors.

climax.text: When you can't predict the future well, spreading bets equally is a powerful default strategy.

quiz.question: Why does 1/N allocation often beat optimized portfolios?
options: Optimization depends on forecasts that are often wrong
Equal division is always mathematically optimal

details.summary: The one-over-N rule allocates resources equally across N options. In investing, it means dividing money equally among all available funds. Despite being maximally simple with zero calculations, it often matches or outperforms optimized portfolio allocation strategies.
details.whyItMatters: The success of one-over-N challenges the assumption that complex optimization produces better outcomes. When future returns are uncertain and estimation error is high, the simplicity of equal allocation provides robustness that outweighs the.
takeaways: Equal allocation across N options requires no estimation or computation
One-over-N matches or beats optimized portfolios in many empirical tests
Estimation error in complex models can be larger than the gains from optimization

faq.question: Why would splitting money equally outperform optimized portfolios?
faq.answer: Optimized portfolios require accurate estimates of future returns, variances, and correlations. When these estimates are wrong, the optimization amplifies the errors. Equal allocation avoids all estimation error, and the robustness gain exceeds the theoretical loss.

faq.question: When should you use the one-over-N rule in practice?
faq.answer: When you have no reliable information to differentiate options, when estimation is unreliable, or when the number of options is modest. It also works as a benchmark: if your complex strategy cannot beat simple equal allocation, the complexity is destroying value.
